value.overview: The Black-cowled Oriole is a medium-sized New World oriole of humid and semi-open habitats in Central America. It is recognized by its bright yellow body, black head and throat, and dark wings and tail. The species commonly occupies forest edges, second-growth vegetation, plantations, gardens, and river corridors rather than dense forest interiors. In Costa Rica, it is a relatively common resident of the Caribbean lowlands and foothills, with occasional occurrences at higher elevations and on the Pacific slope.
value.classification: The Black-cowled Oriole belongs to the oriole family Icteridae and the genus Icterus. Two geographic forms are generally recognized: the nominate Icterus prosthemelas prosthemelas and Icterus prosthemelas praecox, the latter occurring in the southern part of the range, including Costa Rica and Panama.
value.identification: Adults have a vivid yellow body contrasting with a black hood that covers the forehead, face, crown, throat, and upper breast. The wings and tail are mostly black, and the bill is pointed and slightly curved. Females and immature birds are duller, with olive-yellow or yellow-green upperparts and less sharply defined dark areas on the head. The Black-cowled Oriole lacks prominent white wingbars and is smaller and more slender-billed than Audubon's Oriole. Its song is a soft, sweet warble, and its calls can sound harsh and chattering.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Mexico through Belize, Guatemala, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and western Panama. It mainly uses Caribbean lowlands and foothills from sea level to roughly 700 metres in Costa Rica, occasionally reaching about 1,200 metres. In Costa Rica it is relatively common and resident across the Caribbean lowlands, especially along streams and rivers, forest edges, banana plantations, clearings with scattered trees and palms, gardens, and tall secondary growth. Reports also document occurrence on the Pacific slope, where it has expanded or become more regularly detected in lowland areas.
value.migrationStatus: Primarily resident in Costa Rica, especially on the Caribbean slope. Local movements and seasonal dispersal occur, and individuals may be seen outside the core Caribbean range, including on the Pacific slope; it is not considered a long-distance migrant.
value.breeding: Breeding in Costa Rica has been reported mainly from March through July. The nest is a short to deep hanging pouch woven from pale, fine plant fibers. It is usually suspended beneath the central vein or from a folded edge of a banana, palm, or other large leaf, generally about 1.5 to 11 metres above the ground. Some nests may be attached beneath house eaves or to human-made supports. The species often breeds in forest edges, plantations, gardens, and other partly open habitats.
value.dietFeeding: Black-cowled Orioles eat mainly fruit, supplemented by insects and flower nectar. Important nectar sources may include legumes, citrus, agaves, and yuccas. They forage actively in trees, shrubs, plantations, and flowering plants, and may obtain nectar by piercing the base of a flower rather than entering through the opening. They also search foliage and epiphytes for insects, sometimes prying apart plant material with the bill. Their feeding habits can contribute to seed dispersal and insect control.
value.behavior: This is a diurnal, primarily arboreal oriole that often forages around habitat edges and in scattered trees. It may occur alone or in pairs, while juveniles and family groups sometimes travel in small flocks. During the nonbreeding season it can join mixed groups of orioles. The species is generally quiet and can be overlooked, although its soft song and harsh chattering calls are distinctive when heard. At night, groups may roost communally in tall grass or dense vegetation.

conservation.populationTrend: No meaningful global decline is reliably documented; the population is generally considered stable, although local changes may occur as habitat is altered.
